faqs.q: Which RF engineering guide should I read first?
faqs.a: Choose by task rather than publication date. Start with a selection guide when topology is uncertain, a test-report guide when reviewing evidence, or the RFQ guide when specifications are mostly ready. Each article should provide comparison criteria, measurement conditions and a link to the relevant product family.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a duplexer and a diplexer?
faqs.a: A duplexer separates transmit and receive paths so they can share an antenna or port. A diplexer separates or combines different frequency bands. The suitable architecture depends on band plan, port definitions, isolation, insertion loss and power. Use the comparison guide, then submit the band plan through the combiner pathway.

faqs.q: How should a low PIM design guide support product selection?
faqs.a: It should connect PIM targets to frequency, power, connector, material, surface and test conditions rather than present a universal rating. Readers should record the applicable configuration and request supporting PIM evidence. Low PIM performance must be assessed for the specific model and conditions, not generalized across all products.

faqs.q: What should I look for in an RF test report guide?
faqs.a: Look for explanations of test setup, calibration, frequency range, acceptance limits and sample or lot identification. VNA curves, PIM results, reliability tests and matrix-switch automation answer different questions. Coverage must be defined for the applicable product and metric; a sample report shows evidence format, not a universal result.

faqs.q: Can an engineering guide replace a custom RFQ review?
faqs.a: No. A guide helps define topology, specifications and evidence needs, but feasibility still depends on the actual band plan, mechanical envelope, environment and validation requirements. Submit those inputs for review. A complete RFQ can receive initial engineering feedback in about 24 hours, not an automatic quotation or lead-time commitment.
